1.pericope_label: Every high priest taken from among men, who can have compassion on the ignorant

schools.summary: Set out the two qualifications the chapter will test and keep them visible throughout: human sympathy in the first three verses, divine appointment in the fourth. Note that the verb of offering is a present and so denotes offering from time to time, and that the sins offered for include the priest's own in every case the law contemplates. On the two kinds of offering, take the first term for the unbloody offerings of the Law when it stands contrasted with the second, and observe that the Day of Atonement is almost always in this writer's mind, a day on which every offering alike had relation to sins. Reserve the real work for the verb in the second verse. It is a philosophical term, set by Aristotle against the passionlessness the Stoics wanted and used elsewhere of a conqueror's moderation toward the conquered; either apathy or undue severity would disqualify a man for this office.

Explain first why the argument begins with a definition, which will otherwise seem laborious. The new covenant had nothing bodily to show -- no temple, no holy of holies, no priest in great apparel, no legal observances -- and spiritual things do not attract the weak as visible ones do; so the writer starts from the priesthood and sifts the whole matter. Name the difficulty honestly: the one he means to call priest was not well-born, not of the priestly tribe, and never a priest on earth. Then show the method, which is the same he used elsewhere when his readers would not be easily persuaded -- he goes back behind the Law to what happened before it, and opens another path of priesthood altogether.

Lay the definition out in its five clauses and take them one at a time: the priests were taken from among men; they acted not privately but for the whole people; they came furnished with sacrifices and not empty; they were not exempt from human infirmity, so that they might the more readily succour the distressed; and they did not presume to rush into the office. Then say what the passage does not license. The reality found in Christ is here compared with its types, which were prior in time and have now ceased, so that nothing in it supports a continuing sacrifice. On the second verse, do not import the philosophers' sense; the word was used for being indulgent, acting kindly and forbearingly, and that is what is wanted here.

Ground the first clause in the law that required the high priest to be taken from his brethren, then build the twofold scheme the two offerings imply: as the giver of all good God received offerings acknowledging his bounty, and as lawgiver and judge he received sacrifices making atonement. Explain the appointing as what was customary rather than done once, and the phrase about the things of God as bringing God near to men and men to God. On bearing with the ignorant, be exact and be practical: it means bearing with each man in proportion to his ignorance, weakness and circumstances, moderating one's passion when provocation is highest, and administering punishment, where it must fall, in the gentlest manner. Add that weakness excuses nobody who has the means of strength within reach.

Draw the doctrine out of the first clause before expounding anything else. That the priest must be taken from among men implies that man had sinned, that God would not admit sinful man to come to him immediately and alone, that God was pleased to take one from among men by whom they might approach in hope, and that everyone is now welcome who comes by this priest. Make the application at once: let us never attempt to go to God but through Christ, nor expect any favour from God but through Christ. Then keep the purpose in view -- he was ordained for men in things pertaining to God, for the glory of God and the good of men, that he might come between the two.

debates.question: What does the verb rendered "have compassion" mean?

sides.position: A philosophical term set by Aristotle against the passionlessness of the Stoics, and used elsewhere of a conqueror's moderation toward the conquered; here only in the New Testament
The philosophical sense is not quite what is wanted; the lexicographers show it was used for being indulgent, or acting kindly and forgivingly
Not merely to have compassion but to act with moderation, bearing with each in proportion to his ignorance and circumstances, and where punishment must be given, giving it in the gentlest manner
To deal gently with, or more strictly to feel gently towards; either apathy or undue severity would disqualify the man for the office
In proportion to the offence, which is what the Greek word signifies

debates.question: What distinguishes the two kinds of offering?

sides.position: God was regarded in two ways: as giver of all temporal good he received offerings acknowledging his bounty, and as lawgiver and judge he received sacrifices making atonement
The first term denotes the unbloody offerings of the Law when contrasted with the second; on the Day of Atonement all offerings alike had relation to sins
A general term and the bloody offerings, the two together inclusive of all
Out of things inanimate, and animal sacrifices

outliers.note: Alone explains why the argument opens with a definition of priesthood at all, observing that the new covenant had nothing bodily to show -- no temple, no holy of holies, no priest in great apparel, no legal observances -- and that spiritual things do not attract the weak as visible ones do; and alone names the obstacle plainly, that the figure to be called priest was not well-born, not of the sacerdotal tribe, and never a priest on earth.

Alone quotes the description of what a priest must bridle if he is to plead for sinners at all -- his natural disgust at the loathsomeness of sensuality, his impatience at the frequently recurring fall, his hopeless alienation from the hypocrite and the superficial, his indignation at any confession he hears from the penitent -- and alone notes that the priest wears his own weakness lying around him like a chain, adding that Jesus does not.

Alone draws four implications out of the bare requirement that the priest be taken from among men: that man had sinned, that God would not admit sinful man to come to him immediately and alone, that God was pleased to take one from among men by whom they might approach in hope, and that everyone is now welcome who comes by this priest.

themes: For every high priest taken from among men is ordained for men in things pertaining to God, that he may offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins
Who can have compassion on the ignorant, and on them that are out of the way; for that he himself also is compassed with infirmity

3.pericope_label: He ought to offer for his own sins; no man taketh this honour unto himself

schools.summary: Supply the ritual the third verse assumes, since without it the argument is abstract: on the Day of Atonement the high priest brought a sin-offering of a bullock and a burnt-offering of a ram for himself, and for the congregation a sin-offering of two goats with a burnt-offering of a ram; over his own offering he confessed first for himself and his household and then for the priests, while the people's sins were confessed over the goat sent away. Note the small change of preposition from the first verse, which meant nothing in the Greek of the period. On the fourth verse, correct the text -- the true reading gives "when he is called" rather than "he that is called" -- and record what had become of the office by the time of writing, conferred at pleasure and effectively for sale, whatever the law prescribed.

Make the call of God the whole point, since it is what makes any office lawful, and no man can rightly perform one without being made fit for it by God. Then mark the likeness and the difference together: both were called, but one succeeded in a new way and was made a perpetual priest, from which it follows that the older priesthood was temporary and was to cease. Warn against extending Aaron's terms beyond what was decreed, since men concede far more than the Lord granted. And take the general truth the verse yields, which reaches past the priesthood: no government is to be set up in the church by the will of men, but we are to wait for the command of God.

Establish first that the word rendered honour means the office itself, on the usage of the best Greek writers. Then use the verse where it bites. God alone appointed the tribe and family from which the high priest came, and God alone could provide a high priest for the whole race; men had no authority in the matter. Answer the argument some build on this for an unbroken succession of ordainers: no such succession exists or ever did, and even were it granted it would be beside the point, since the text speaks only of an appointment within one tribe and family, that line was itself broken, and the office was to cease with the coming of Christ, who can have no successor and needs no vicar. Close on the summary this chapter is working toward -- whatever is excellent in the Levitical priesthood is in Christ more eminently, and whatever is wanting in those priests is in him.

debates.question: What may be built on "no man taketh this honour unto himself"?

sides.position: That the call of God is what makes any office lawful; and since Christ's priesthood was perpetual and Aaron's was not, the older priesthood was temporary. No government may be set up in the church by the will of men

Nothing supporting an unbroken succession of ordainers: no such succession exists or did, and the text speaks only of an appointment within one tribe and family, itself broken, the office ceasing with Christ, who can have no successor
The call meant is external rather than inward, and the verse has no reference to the Christian ministry and should not be applied to it
The modern minister is not a priest, but he should still be a God-called man and not one who pushes himself into office

outliers.note: Alone supplies the ritual the verse assumes, the bullock and ram for the high priest himself and the two goats and ram for the congregation, with confession made first for himself and his household, then for the priests, and the people's sins confessed over the goat sent into the wilderness.

Alone turns the verse into an attack on the doctrine of an uninterrupted succession of ordainers, calling it a fable invented by ecclesiastical tyrants, and arguing that even if it were true it would be beside the point, since the passage speaks only of an appointment within one tribe and family, that line was itself broken, and the office was to cease with the coming of Christ.

Alone catalogues what made the office honourable -- the anointing, the garments, the maintenance, the retinue and the reverence -- and then subordinates all of it to the work itself, in which the priests were types.

themes: And by reason hereof he ought, as for the people, so also for himself, to offer for sins
And no man taketh this honour unto himself, but he that is called of God, as was Aaron

5.pericope_label: Christ glorified not himself; thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec

schools.summary: The verb of glorifying has to be carried over from the previous clause, so read the sentence as saying that God glorified him in appointing him. Then handle the two quotations. The first is about sonship rather than priesthood, and the connection is worth naming: where the Pentateuch gives the high priest a distinctive title it almost always calls him the anointed priest, so the single name "the Christ" already unites the two testimonies that follow. The second is the crucial text on which the whole later argument rests, though at this stage the only point pressed is the fact of divine appointment. Note that it says priest where the argument wants high priest, and that the writer treats the words as synonymous. Mention, without settling, the question whether the priesthood is coeval with the sonship or merely fitting because of it.

Admit the difficulty before answering it: being begotten of God does not of itself make a man a priest, so the first quotation may look far-fetched. The answer is that the begetting spoken of there was a testimony rendered before men, so the question becomes what sort of Son was manifested -- not one endued with no honour or power, but a Mediator between God and man; and on that showing the begetting included the priesthood. Reduce the verse to its proposition: Christ did not make himself a high priest, but God made him one. On the second quotation, meet the evasion head on. Those who apply the psalm to David show extreme effrontery, for kings might not exercise the priesthood, and Uzziah was struck with leprosy for that single act of intermeddling; the comparison with a man who was both priest and king leaves nothing doubtful.

Say plainly that the man Jesus was appointed to this office as Aaron was, and then draw the contrast the older priesthood cannot survive. The Jewish high priest represented the offering by the blood of beasts; this one had to offer his own life, and having risen he appears in the presence of God for us. Because he never dies he can never have a successor, and can have no vicars in heaven or on earth; those who claim to be such are impostors. Add the temporal point that makes it stick: a priest for ever, as long as sun and moon endure, admits no succession of priests at all. On the order named at the close, be honest -- who Melchizedek was must still remain a secret, and nothing more is known of him than the few verses in Genesis. And note the one caution about the day named in the psalm: it is not the moment of the appointing, the generation being from eternity.

debates.question: How is a quotation about sonship evidence about priesthood?

sides.position: The begetting spoken of was a testimony rendered before men, so the question is what sort of Son was manifested: one who was to be Mediator, and his begetting therefore included his priesthood
Where the Pentateuch gives the high priest a distinctive title it is almost always "the anointed priest," so the one name "the Christ" unites both testimonies that follow
The language of the psalm is general enough to apply to any exaltation of the Redeemer, and is used here with strict propriety
Scholars differ: one holds the priesthood coeval with the sonship, another that it is merely suitable because he is Son; the Father clearly nominated him to it
The day named is not the moment of the appointment, the generation being from eternity

outliers.note: Alone unites the chapter's two quotations through a single title, observing that where the Pentateuch gives the high priest a distinctive designation it is almost always "the anointed priest," so that the name "the Christ" already holds together the Anointed King addressed as Son and the same figure addressed as priest for ever.

Alone admits that the first quotation may look far-fetched, since being begotten of God does not of itself make a priest, and alone answers the evasion that applies the second psalm to David, calling it extreme effrontery on the ground that kings might not exercise the priesthood, and citing Uzziah struck with leprosy for that one act of intermeddling.

Alone presses the perpetuity into a polemical conclusion, that a priest for ever admits no succession of priests and can have no vicars in heaven or on earth, those who pretend to be such being impostors; and alone says outright of Melchizedek that who he was must still remain a secret.

themes: So also Christ glorified not himself to be made an high priest; but he that said unto him, Thou art my Son, to day have I begotten thee
Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec

7.pericope_label: Strong crying and tears; though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience

schools.summary: Locate the scene, since the passage is about a particular hour: this is Gethsemane, though other occasions of weeping are not excluded. Give the word for supplication its force -- it is formed from the noun for a suppliant and suggests a man coming with an olive branch, and it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. Then answer the question the verse forces, what was granted, since the death was not averted; take the reverence named at the close as the attitude of one who surrendered his will at once and was thereby enabled to acquiesce. Note that the clause about sonship may attach to what precedes, in which case the hearing was granted for the reverent fear and not because he was in the pre-eminent sense a Son. On the learning of obedience, point out that the two verbs play on each other in the Greek, and say what growth can and cannot mean: he always did his Father's will, but grew in experience as in wisdom and stature.

Name the two ends the suffering served and keep them apart: the proximate, that he might learn obedience, and the ultimate, that he might be consecrated a priest for our salvation. Then guard the phrase about the days of his flesh, which has been abused. The word denotes a condition and not a substance, so those who conclude from it that he is now divested of flesh are raving; it is one thing to be a real man endued with blessed immortality, another to be liable to the sorrows he bore while here and has now laid aside. On the learning, deny the wrong picture firmly: he was not driven to it by force nor exercised as oxen and horses are when their ferocity is tamed, being already willing. Yet it may truly be said that by his death he learned what obeying costs, since he then denied himself in a special manner. Close with the use -- the yoke is shaken off in prosperity, and it is the cross that makes us obedient.

Warn the hearers at the outset that this is among the hardest places in the epistle, that the labour of learned men on it has been prodigious, and that their meaning is often hard to find. Then be concrete about the passion: the days meant are the two in which the suffering stood at its height, the prayers were offered three times, the strong crying and tears belong to the garden. Answer the question of the hearing directly -- he was heard, not so that the cup should pass, but so that he drank it. And say what was most dreaded, which was not the shameful death, terrible as its image was, but the weight of infinite justice, the being bruised and put to grief by the hand of God himself; beside that everything else was a mere nothing. Add that throughout the whole life it was never the suffering he was to undergo but the dishonour sin had done to so holy a God that grieved that spotless soul.

debates.question: What does "the days of his flesh" imply about the present?

sides.position: Nothing material: the word denotes a condition, and those who conclude the flesh has been laid aside are raving; it is one thing to be a real man endued with blessed immortality, another to be liable to the sorrows he bore here
It is not to be concluded that he has no flesh now, since he had flesh after the resurrection; only its infirmities are gone
The Son is still united to human nature, but it is human nature glorified
The time of the incarnation, when he took all the infirmities of human nature upon him, sinful passions excepted
Those two days in particular in which his sufferings were at the height

debates.question: In what sense was he heard, since the death was not averted?

sides.position: He was heard, not so that the cup should pass, but so that he drank it; what he most dreaded was the weight of infinite justice, not the shameful death
He surrendered his will at once to the Father, who heard his plea and enabled him to acquiesce in that will
The hearing may have been granted for his reverent fear rather than because he was, in the pre-eminent sense, God's Son

outliers.note: Alone concedes the difficulty before attempting it, calling this one of the most difficult places in the epistle if not in the whole New Testament, the labours of learned men upon it prodigious, and their meaning hard to find even so.

Alone answers the question of what was granted in the hearing -- that he was heard, not so that the cup should pass, but so that he drank it -- and alone identifies what was most dreaded as the weight of infinite justice rather than the shameful death, adding that throughout the life it was the dishonour sin had done to God, and not the suffering, that grieved that soul.

Alone separates the proximate end of the suffering from the ultimate, that he might learn obedience and that he might be consecrated a priest; and alone denies the wrong picture of that learning in so many words, that he was not driven to it by force nor exercised as oxen and horses are when their ferocity is to be tamed.

Alone points out the play the Greek makes between the verb for learning and the verb for suffering, and alone derives the word for supplication from the noun for a suppliant, suggesting one who comes carrying an olive branch.

themes: Who in the days of his flesh, when he had offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears... and was heard in that he feared
Though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered

9.pericope_label: Being made perfect, the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him

schools.summary: Guard the participle rendered "made perfect" before anything else: what was completed was fitness to save, not moral perfection, since there was never any sin; it is the finishing of a training carried on by means of sufferings. Then take the closing verb carefully, because it is not the ordinary word for appointing. It means to salute or address, occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and is common in Plutarch, so the verse does not say the man was appointed at this point but that he was so addressed, namely in the psalm. Note what the quotation does with its source -- where the psalm said priest the text now says high priest -- and be candid that nothing in the argument turns on it, the Hebrew word covering both. Observe finally that the repetition of the earlier words at the close of the paragraph is deliberate and impressive, and that the long digression which follows is not really a digression at all.

Prefer "consecrated" to "made perfect": the Greek will bear either, but where the subject is priesthood the language of sanctification fits, as when he said he sanctified himself for their sakes; and the term applies properly to the human nature, in which the office was discharged and the suffering borne. Then state the doctrine the verse carries and do not soften it. The writer does not offer Christ merely as an example but ascends higher, to an obedience which blotted out our transgressions and obtained righteousness for us before God, the disobedience of Adam being removed by an act of the contrary kind. It follows that the sufferings are no prejudice to his dignity but his glory, for if salvation is highly esteemed by us, how honourably ought we to think of its author. On the order of Melchizedek, note the resemblances that make the comparison fit: the absence of recorded parentage, the manner of the instalment, and the antiquity and perpetuity of the office.

This is the verse on which to be explicit about the terms of salvation, and the sources leave no room for vagueness. He tasted death for every man, but he is the author of eternal salvation only to those who obey him; it is not merely believers but obedient believers who are finally saved. State the threefold summary plainly -- that obedience to Christ is as necessary to salvation as believing on him, that he was perfected as high priest by offering himself a sacrifice for sin, and that by the merit of that sacrifice he obtained pardon and eternal life for those who obey. Say what follows: on this text no man is saved by an obedience of Christ's merely reckoned to him. Gloss the obeying as doing and suffering his whole will. On the closing verb, note that it properly means surnamed, and that who Melchizedek was seems to have been concealed on purpose, so that he might be the more eminent type.

Prepare the hearers for what is coming rather than expounding at length, since the writer himself is about to break off. Say that there are many things to be said concerning this mysterious person whose priesthood was eternal, and that the salvation procured by it is therefore eternal also. Report the view that what was hard to be uttered concerned not Melchizedek himself but the one of whom he was the type, and grant its force: there are great mysteries in the person and offices of the Redeemer, and Christianity is itself the great mystery of godliness. Then name the reason the writer gives for holding back, which is not the difficulty of the subject but the dullness of the hearers -- and let that stand as the transition into what follows.

debates.question: What does "unto all them that obey him" establish?

sides.position: That he tasted death for every man but is the author of salvation only to those who obey; not believers but obedient believers are finally saved, which is unimpeachable evidence that no man is saved by an obedience of Christ's reckoned to him
The opposite: the writer does not offer Christ merely as an example but ascends higher, to an obedience that blotted out our transgressions and obtained righteousness for us before God
That this is not to save those who live in sin; only those who obey him have any evidence that they will be saved
Obeying means doing and suffering his whole will
He presents to all the model of the obedience to be rendered to him, and through him to the Father

debates.question: What does the verb at the close of the paragraph mean?

sides.position: To salute or address; it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and is common in Plutarch
Not that he was appointed to the office in the sense we often use, but simply that he was so addressed, namely in the psalm
Being constituted, hailed and acknowledged, as those accosting a newly made king would hail him as king
It properly signifies surnamed
Addressed rather than called; and note that the psalm's "priest" is here altered to "high priest," which is what brings its meaning fully out

outliers.note: Alone takes the clause about obeying as decisive against imputed obedience, holding that Christ tasted death for every man but is the author of eternal salvation only to those who obey, so that it is not believers but obedient believers who are finally saved.

Alone argues the contrary from the same verse, that the writer does not offer Christ merely as an example but ascends higher, to an obedience which blotted out our transgressions and obtained righteousness for us before God, the disobedience of Adam being removed by an act of the opposite kind.

Alone observes what the quotation does to its source, that the psalm's "priest" is here altered to "high priest" and that the change is what brings the psalm's meaning fully out, and alone remarks that the long passage which follows can hardly be called a digression given the practical aim of the epistle.
Alone suspects that who Melchizedek was has been concealed on purpose, so that he might be the more eminent type of Christ.

themes: And being made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him
Called of God an high priest after the order of Melchisedec

11.pericope_label: Many things hard to be uttered, seeing ye are dull of hearing

schools.summary: Correct the familiar rendering first: the adjective means hard to interpret, not hard to utter, and it is a rare compound found in two Greek authors and nowhere else in the New Testament. Then explain the word for dullness, built on a negative and a verb meaning to push -- no push in the hearing, sluggish in mind as much as in ear, a word Plato used of stupid students. Say what can and cannot be recovered about the charge: nobody now knows what particular fact grounded it. On the expectation that they should be teaching by this time, read it modestly -- not that all should preach, but that all should be able to explain the faith to a child or a neighbour; and note that the verse proves these were not recent converts. Take "the oracles of God" as the Old Testament scriptures, on the usage of the New Testament and of Philo, and note that the noun is a diminutive, divine utterances being usually brief.

Locate the difficulty where the writer locates it, not in the subject but in the hearers. The Lord speaks to us so clearly that his word is rightly called our light; it is our darkness that dims the brightness. Distinguish the two possible senses of the reproof and take the harder: to be dull in the ears would mean inattentive, but to be sluggish in them means slowness of comprehension. Then deliver the rebuke in the form the text gives it -- you do not know the alphabet -- and immediately guard it, since we must go on learning through life, and only the man who owns himself far from perfect knowledge is truly wise. What is condemned is not learning but remaining always among the first principles. Add the sharp point: not years only but days must be accounted for, and few of us call ourselves to any account for past time.

Settle what the many things concern, and give the reason for your choice. It is unlikely to be Melchizedek, since the seventh chapter says far more about him and says it plainly, and the readers could hardly have grown more capable in the hours between; so take it of Christ, or of that endless priesthood, which carnal Christians do not easily grasp. Then correct the grammar of the twelfth verse: the pronoun is accusative, so the sense is that someone must teach them a second time certain elements. Read the words as implying that they had once been better taught and had forgotten, having probably given up hearing the gospel altogether -- which is precisely why the letter was written, to reclaim backsliders and preserve them from total apostasy. Explain the milk as the metaphor authors sacred and profane use for first principles, sucking standing for learning.

Keep this brief and lay the responsibility where it belongs. There is a difficulty in the things themselves, and there may be a weakness in ministers when they try to speak clearly about them, but generally the fault is in the hearers: dull hearers make the preaching of the gospel a difficult thing. Add that even those who have some faith may be dull hearers and slow to believe, so that nobody in the congregation is exempt from the charge by being a believer. Then state the measure by which they are judged, which is the measure by which all are judged: much is looked for from those to whom much is given.

debates.question: Whom or what are the many hard things about?

sides.position: Not Melchizedek, since the seventh chapter says far more about him and says it plainly; rather Christ, or that endless priesthood which carnal Christians cannot easily grasp
The likeness of Jesus as high priest to Melchizedek; the pronoun may be masculine or neuter
The whole subject, Christ made high priest after the order of Melchizedek
Melchizedek, or Christ, or his priesthood, or all of these
Not in the subject but in the hearers: the Lord speaks so clearly that his word is called our light, and its brightness is dimmed by our darkness
Not so much in the subject matter as in their slothfulness in considering and dulness in apprehending
Partly in the strange line taken, which ran counter to Jewish ideas, but still more in their dulness
There is difficulty in the things themselves and weakness in ministers, but generally the fault is in the hearers
Their faculty of hearing had once been acute; a lack of interest has come upon them, and with it a want of power

outliers.note: Alone argues against referring the many hard things to Melchizedek, on the practical ground that the seventh chapter says far more about him and says it plainly, and that the readers could hardly have grown more capable in the few hours between the writing of the two chapters.

Alone locates the difficulty in a doctrine of illumination rather than in the subject, saying that the Lord speaks so clearly that his word is rightly called our light and that its brightness becomes dim through our darkness; and alone insists that not years only but days must be accounted for.

Alone dates the reproof, counting about thirty years from Pentecost and listing the advantages enjoyed -- descent from Abraham, the law and the writings, in some cases the ministry of Christ or of his apostles -- so that the dulness is aggravated by the time available.
Alone breaks off to apply the verse to his own readers, remarking of the phrase about the time elapsed: what a commentary on modern Christians.

themes: Of whom we have many things to say, and hard to be uttered, seeing ye are dull of hearing
For when for the time ye ought to be teachers, ye have need that one teach you again which be the first principles of the oracles of God

13.pericope_label: Milk and strong meat; senses exercised to discern both good and evil

schools.summary: Note the shift the English hides -- the complaint has moved from needing milk to living on it by choice, so that the readers stand self-confessed as infants. Take the adjective as inexperienced rather than unskilful, and add the caution that it does not question whether they were Christians, only whether they had experience enough for the higher matters. On "the word of righteousness," report the disagreement rather than settling it quietly, and if you take it for developed Christian teaching as such, admit that the choice of word needs explaining, righteousness not being this epistle's manifest subject. Then give the closing verse its precision: the perfection is relative, of adults rather than absolute; the word for senses is the Stoics' term for the organs of perception, and an ancient physician uses the very phrase found here; and the skill is for deciding between good and evil, gained by use.

Read the infancy as one of understanding, and put it in a phrase they will remember: it constrains God to prattle with us. Guard it at once -- a grown man is not averse to milk, only to living on nothing else. Then take a position on "the word of righteousness" and defend it: the apostle is not here raising the question how we are justified before God, but using the word in a simpler sense for that completeness of knowledge which leads on to maturity. On the discerning of good and evil, make the point defensively rather than as an ornament. We cannot be rightly taught unless we are fortified against the delusions of Satan, for a faith suspended between truth and falsehood may come to nothing at any moment; and it is not the mind alone but all the senses that are named, to show we must strive until we are in every way furnished by God's word. And distinguish the perfections: not of justification, since babes in Christ are as perfectly justified as the grown, nor of holiness, which is imperfect in all here, but of knowledge.

Take the milk for the doctrines of the law, the rudiments meant to lead us to Christ, and the word of righteousness for the doctrine of justification, so that the man who rests in ceremonies is inexperienced in it -- but note that another reading runs the other way, making the milk-fed those who can digest nothing but justification and imputed righteousness. State which you take. Then list what the solid food actually consists of, and do not be abstract: the atonement, justification by faith, the gift of the Holy Ghost, the fullness of Christ dwelling in the soul, triumph over death, the resurrection of the body, and the glorification of both body and soul. On the senses being exercised, enumerate the organs one by one and say that something in the soul answers to each of them; the habit meant is strength of spiritual understanding arising from maturity, by which such men exercise themselves with ease, readiness and cheerfulness.

sides.position: The doctrine of justification: the man who lives on milk rests in the ceremonies of the law and is inexperienced in justification, which requires faith in the sacrificial death
Not the question how we are justified before God at all, but the completeness of knowledge that leads on to maturity
The sublimer truths of the gospel; the milk-fed are precisely those who desire and can digest nothing but justification and imputed righteousness
The doctrine respecting the way in which men become righteous
Complete, properly developed Christian teaching; though the choice of the word needs explaining, righteousness not being this epistle's manifest subject
Perhaps moral truth is meant

debates.question: What perfection is meant by "of full age"?

sides.position: Not of justification, since babes in Christ are as perfectly justified as the grown; nor of sanctification, there being no perfect holiness here; nor of parts, which infants have as truly: it is a perfection of knowledge
Relative perfection, the word being used of adults in contrast with babes, not absolute perfection
Those who are adults, called men in Christ by a figure, that is, the spiritual
Those who by long experience can appreciate the more elevated doctrines and distinguish them from error

outliers.note: Alone notices that the complaint has shifted from needing milk to making it the sole food by choice, and alone guesses at the situation behind it, a temptation to mingle rudimentary Christian doctrine with the teaching of the synagogue, which would have cost them the elements of Christian truth and any real knowledge of the older scriptures besides.

Alone describes the infancy as one that constrains God to prattle with us, and alone makes the discerning of good and evil a defensive necessity rather than an ornament, since a faith suspended between truth and falsehood is in danger of coming to nothing at any moment.

Alone distinguishes the perfections that are not meant -- not of justification, since babes in Christ are as perfectly justified as the grown, nor of sanctification, nor of parts -- before settling on a perfection of knowledge.

Alone corrects the figure's application, insisting that it is not of eaters who by long use tell good food from bad but of experienced Christians who tell useful teaching from injurious, and calling the result a delicate taste for the doctrines that impart light and consolation.

themes: For every one that useth milk is unskilful in the word of righteousness: for he is a babe
But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil
